classification.difficultyReason: Compare two graphical models of break-even, then form a profit expression and interpret integer solutions to loss and profit inequalities.

content.prompt: [Break-even point] A certain business has fixed costs of $\$900$ plus costs of $\$30$ per item sold. The sale price of each item is $\$50$. If enough items are sold then the company is just able to pay its total costs. That point is called the break-even point. Companies may use several different methods to graph this information. Here are two such methods. In each case, let $n$ be the number of items sold.

children.label: i
children.prompt: The gross profit per item is $\$50-\$30=\$20$. Sketch the graph of the gross profit for $n$ items where $y=\$20\times n$.

answer.worked: Plot $(0,0)$ and $(20,400)$, then draw the straight line $y=20n$ for $n\geq0$. The vertical coordinate is measured in dollars.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: On the same graph, sketch the fixed costs $y=\$900$.

answer.worked: Draw a horizontal line through $(0,900)$ on the graph from part a i.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: The point where these two lines cross is the break-even point. How many items need to be sold to break even?

answer.worked: The lines intersect at $(45,900)$, so 45 items must be sold to break even.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 15a; teacher PDF page 23 lower-right answer region
spec.description: Shared solution graph for a i and a ii. A rising gross-profit line and horizontal fixed-cost line intersect at n=45.
spec.mathematics: y=20n and y=900, n nonnegative; intersection (45,900). Teacher tick labels n=20,40 and y=400,800 are retained.

children.label: i
children.prompt: On a new graph, draw $y=\$50\times n$, the total sales for $n$ items.

answer.worked: Plot $(0,0)$ and $(40,2000)$, then draw the straight line $y=50n$ for $n\geq0$. The vertical coordinate is measured in dollars.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: On the same graph, draw $y=\$900+\$30\times n$, the total cost for $n$ items.

answer.worked: Plot $(0,900)$ and $(40,2100)$, then draw the straight line $y=900+30n$ on the graph from part b i.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: Does the break-even point for this graph agree with the result of part a?

answer.short: Yes. Both give $n=45$ items; total sales and total cost are each $\$2250$.
answer.worked: The sales and total-cost lines intersect at $(45,2250)$. Thus break-even occurs at 45 items, agreeing with part a. The vertical coordinates differ because the two methods graph different quantities.

spec.sourceRegion: Question 15b; teacher PDF page 23 lower-right answer region
spec.description: Shared solution graph for b i and b ii. Sales and total-cost lines intersect at (45,2250). Close vertical tick labels 900 and 1000 are offset to preserve readability.
spec.mathematics: y=50n and y=900+30n, n nonnegative. Teacher tick labels n=20,40 and y=900,1000,2000,3000 are retained.

children.label: c
children.prompt: The net profit is the income from sales minus the cost. A positive net profit indicates that the business makes a profit and a negative net profit indicates a loss.

children.label: i
children.prompt: Write down a formula for the net profit $\$P$ in terms of $n$.

children.label: ii
children.prompt: The company has sufficient funds to cover a loss of up to $\$400$ and still stay in business. How many items are sold if the company does indeed remain in business?

answer.worked:
A loss of up to $\$400$ means $P\geq-400$.

$$\begin{align*}20n-900&\geq-400\\20n&\geq500\\n&\geq25\end{align*}$$

At least 25 items must be sold.

children.label: iii
children.prompt: The company has a profit target of $\$750$. How many items are sold given that the company exceeds the profit target?

answer.short:
At least 83 items: $n\geq83$.

The strict profit inequality gives $n>82.5$; the number of items is a whole number.
answer.worked:
$$\begin{align*}20n-900&>750\\20n&>1650\\n&>\frac{165}{2}\\n&>82.5\end{align*}$$

Since $n$ is a whole number, at least 83 items are sold.
